studies.Reference: Soy and isoflavone intake are associated with reduced risk of ovarian cancer in southeast china.
studies.Authors: Zhang M, Xie X, Lee AH, Binns CW
studies.exposure_measurement_supporting_text: Habitual dietary intakes including 9 soy foods were measured by face-to-face interview using a validated and reliable food-frequency questionnaire.

extraction_supporting_text.sample_size: Cases were 254 patients with histologically confirmed epithelial ovarian cancer. The 652 controls comprised 340 hospital visitors, 261 non-neoplastic hospital outpatients, and 51 women recruited from the community.
extraction_supporting_text.effect_size: Compared with the highest versus the lowest quartile intake, the ORs were 0.50 (95% CI = 0.31-0.82) for total soy foods
extraction_supporting_text.effect_direction: Intake of soy and isoflavones was inversely related to the risk of ovarian cancer.
extraction_supporting_text.p_value: Computed from the reported effect and 95% CI using a normal approximation: p=0.005.
extraction_supporting_text.outcome_definition: Cases were 254 patients with histologically confirmed epithelial ovarian cancer.
extraction_supporting_text.exposure_definition: Habitual dietary intakes including 9 soy foods were measured by face-to-face interview using a validated and reliable food-frequency questionnaire.

studies.Reference: Soy and isoflavone intake associated with reduced risk of ovarian cancer in southern Chinese women.
studies.Authors: Lee AH, Su D, Pasalich M, Tang L, Binns CW, Qiu L
studies.comparison_type: Highest vs Lowest (≥120 g/day vs <61 g/day)
studies.exposure_measurement_supporting_text: Information on habitual consumption of soy foods, including soybean, soy milk, fresh tofu, dried tofu, and soybean sprout, was obtained face-to-face from participants through a validated and reliable semi-quantitative food frequency questionnaire.

extraction_supporting_text.sample_size: Five hundred incident patients with histologically confirmed cancer of the ovary and 500 controls (mean age 59 years) were recruited from four public hospitals in Guangzhou.
extraction_supporting_text.effect_size: the adjusted odds ratio being 0.29 (95% confidence interval 0.20 to 0.42) for women who consumed at least 120 g/day relative to those less than 61 g/day
extraction_supporting_text.effect_direction: regular intake of soy foods could reduce the ovarian cancer risk; consumption of soy foods is associated with a reduced risk of ovarian cancer
extraction_supporting_text.outcome_definition: Five hundred incident patients with histologically confirmed cancer of the ovary
extraction_supporting_text.exposure_definition: habitual consumption of soy foods, including soybean, soy milk, fresh tofu, dried tofu, and soybean sprout; total soy foods (75.3 ± 53.6 g/day) compared to the controls (110.7 ± 88.8 g/day)

headline.funnel_interpretation: Insufficient studies to perform formal publication bias testing.
headline.results_interpretation: The pooled analysis of 2 studies yielded an overall effect size of 0.41 (95% CI: 0.25–0.67), suggesting that soy is associated with a lower risk of ovarian cancer. However, this association should be interpreted with caution, as there was substantial between-study heterogeneity (I² = 67.64%), reflecting considerable variability across studies.
